title: A son is born
hookLine: news of his son arrives; the child is named Rahula, "a fetter"
carry: love, and the fear inside it
last: SAMANA — THERE IS ANOTHER WAY TO LIVE.

cards: A messenger is hurrying down the road with news from the palace. In the stories, the prince is riding home from the park, the fourth sight still shining in his mind, when the messenger reaches him.
Yasodhara has given birth. You have a son. New parents sometimes describe two things arriving at once: a love bigger than they expected, and right behind it, the fear of losing what they love.
The prince, the stories say, answers with a strange sentence. Not a cheer. Something closer to a sigh.

teach.h: A RAHULA IS BORN — A FETTER.
teach.b: What the prince says, in the later telling, is: a rahula is born, a fetter is born. A bond. Something that ties me down.
The king hears it and names the baby Rahula. It sounds harsh to modern ears, and people read it more than one way.

teach.h: A FATHER TORN, OR PLAIN HONESTY?
teach.b: Some hear a father torn: he has just glimpsed another way to live, and now a child holds him to this one. Others hear plain honesty about love. He doesn't say the baby is bad.
He says the love is binding.

Some scholars add that the name may once have meant something else, perhaps tied to Rahu, the shadow that swallows the moon in an eclipse, and the fetter story may explain a name that came first. The timing differs too.
In the Pali commentaries, Rahula is born the day his father leaves. In some northern Buddhist tellings, he's born years later, on the night of the awakening.
The sources disagree, and that's fine to say.
Underneath it all is a feeling: love, and the fear inside it. Buddhism doesn't say stop loving. It says look closely at the gripping, the part that wants to hold so tight nothing can ever change.

teach.h: LOVE, AND THE FEAR INSIDE IT.
teach.b: And Rahula doesn't vanish from the story. He comes back, and the Buddha himself will teach him. Now look back at this week: three palaces, Yasodhara, four sights, and a son.
Everything the prince has, and everything he is about to leave.

how: Buddhists tell the story of Rahula's birth as part of the going forth, and Buddhist parents are taught to love fully while practicing non-attachment, which means not clinging, rather than not caring.

o: a palace servant who carried the royal news
the prince's son, whose name means a fetter
a royal title meaning heir to the throne

games.q: what's inside the name — tap the pairs.
p: the shadow that swallows the moon

s: every Buddhist tradition says Rahula was born the night his father left
the Pali commentaries say so; some northern tellings put his birth years later, on the night of the awakening.
the prince's sentence was a fetter is born
in the later telling, a rahula, a fetter, is born, and the king makes it the child's name.
Buddhism teaches parents to stop loving
it teaches loosening the grip, not the love.

games.q: you're the prince, riding home, and a messenger says you have a son. what comes out of your mouth?
o: a shout of joy for the whole city.
a rahula is born: a fetter is born.
nothing: you ride home in silence.
games.why: in the telling, he names the tie out loud. the king hears it and calls the child Rahula.

practice: Hold something you love in your hand: a mug, a photo, a stone from a beach, or simply your own other hand. Close your fingers tight around it for a breath or two and feel the tension climb your arm.
Then slowly loosen until it rests in an open palm, still yours, still loved, just not squeezed, and breathe with the difference between holding and gripping.

wordCard.voice: Rahula. The Buddha's son, whose name, in the old telling, means a fetter: the tie of love that holds us.

orig.note: Pali: the name of the Buddha's son, explained in the commentaries as a fetter or bond.

carryVoice: Your line: love, and the fear inside it. Loosening the grip is not letting go of the love. The palace week, done.
